cases.brief: Should we move our weekly all-hands meeting to Monday mornings, or keep it on Friday afternoons? Attendance has been slipping and the team is split on the change.
Should we hire a second support engineer this quarter, or wait until January?
Should our 12-person startup move to a four-day work week, or keep five days?
Should we sponsor the industry conference in March, or skip it this year?
Should we renew our office lease for two years, or go fully remote?
Should we raise our subscription price by 10% next quarter, or hold it steady?

Should we replace our current CRM with HubSpot next quarter, or keep what we have? We are a 34-person B2B sales team. Annual CRM cost is about £50,000 and switching would cost roughly £20,000 one-off. The goal is higher sales productivity without blowing the budget.

Should we outsource our payroll to an external provider, or keep it in-house? Payroll admin currently costs us about £85,000 a year in staff time, and the provider quotes £3,000 a month plus a £10,000 setup fee. We are worried about error rates and losing control of our data.

Should we open a second warehouse in Manchester next year, or expand our existing site? A new site would cost roughly £1.2 million up front with £300,000 a year in running costs; expanding the current one is about £450,000. Faster delivery to northern customers is the main prize.

Should we switch our 40-person engineering team from quarterly releases to continuous deployment? Release overhead currently eats about two engineer-days per sprint, but several enterprise customers say they value predictable, well-documented quarterly release notes.

Should we launch our beta programme in September with 50 hand-picked customers, or wait for the polished full release in December? Early feedback would shape the roadmap while it can still change, but a buggy beta could damage our reputation with the key accounts we most need to impress.

Should we enter the German market next year via a local distributor, our own sales office, or an acquisition of a small local reseller? We are a UK industrial-sensors firm with £8 million revenue. A Munich office would cost about £600,000 in year one and give us full control of the brand, but hiring is slow and we have no local network. The distributor route costs almost nothing up front but surrenders roughly 35% margin and risks weak commitment — our Nordic distributor generated only a fifth of its forecast. Acquiring the reseller we know would cost around £1.5 million and bring 12 experienced people plus 200 accounts, but integration would distract engineering leadership for months. Board members disagree strongly: the CFO wants the low-risk distributor path, while the sales director insists only direct presence wins the big automotive contracts we actually need.

Should we rewrite our ten-year-old monolithic platform as microservices, modernise it incrementally module by module, or leave the architecture alone and spend the effort on features? The monolith serves 900 enterprise tenants with 99.9% uptime, but deployments take four hours, onboarding a new engineer takes three months, and two of our five most senior engineers have threatened to leave over the state of the codebase. A full rewrite is estimated at 18 months with feature development largely frozen — and our main competitor ships monthly. Incremental modernisation avoids the freeze but past attempts stalled twice when product deadlines intervened. Doing nothing preserves velocity today but our defect rate has doubled year on year, and the last major outage cost us a flagship customer. Engineering, product and the CEO each favour a different option, and morale is fragile.

Should we electrify our 45-vehicle delivery fleet over the next two years, or run the existing diesel vans until 2030? Replacing all 45 vans costs about £1.8 million, partly offset by a government grant worth up to £225,000 that expires next year. Fuel and maintenance savings are estimated at £280,000 a year, but our depot needs £150,000 of charging infrastructure and the local grid connection may add six months of delay. Diesel keeps capital free for the warehouse automation project the operations director champions, but the city centre we serve introduces a clean-air charge in 2028 of roughly £60,000 a year, and two major retail customers have started asking about our emissions in tender documents. Drivers are split: some love the new vans, others fear range problems on rural rounds. The board wants a defensible recommendation this quarter.

Should we move our B2B software pricing from per-seat licences to usage-based pricing, offer both models side by side, or keep per-seat and simply raise prices 8% at renewal? Per-seat brings in £4.2 million a year and is predictable, but seat counts have stagnated and three of our ten largest customers cut seats at the last renewal, costing about £190,000. Usage-based pricing could grow revenue from our heaviest users — our top decile consumes 40 times the median — but finance fears revenue volatility and our billing system would need roughly £120,000 of work plus four months of integration. Running both models risks confusing the sales team and inviting every renewal into a repricing negotiation. Sales, finance and product each back a different option, churn is creeping up, and we have promised investors a decision before the next board meeting.

Should we build our own applicant-tracking capability into our HR platform, partner deeply with the market leader, or acquire the struggling five-person startup whose product our customers already love? Building in-house keeps the roadmap under our control and the margin whole, but our engineers estimate a year to reach parity and we have missed our last two roadmap dates. Partnering gets us to market in a quarter with revenue share, but the leader also talks to our biggest competitor and could switch sides. The acquisition would cost somewhere near the top of our available cash, founders may leave after earn-out, and technical due diligence found their codebase depends on a deprecated framework. Meanwhile two large customers have made applicant tracking a renewal condition for next year, and our win rate against the integrated suites has fallen for three consecutive quarters. What should we do?

I need to work out whether we push into Germany next year or double down on the UK — that's the decision, and honestly the board is split. We're an 85-person regtech SaaS doing £11.2m ARR, growing about 28% year on year, but UK new-logo growth slowed to 9% over the last two quarters and I think the UK market is maybe 70% penetrated for our segment — that's my gut, not a real number. The goal is to get to £20m ARR by end of FY28 without dropping gross margin below 78%. Germany: TAM is supposedly €400m (that's from the 2025 Gartner regtech sizing, though our head of sales thinks it's inflated, maybe half that once you strip out the banks we can't serve). BaFin licensing will take 9 to 14 months, legal quoted us €250k for the process, and we'd need maybe 6 local hires — say €900k a year fully loaded. We have £3.1m cash and we're profitable-ish, breakeven plus or minus £100k a quarter, so we can't fund a two-year burn on this. Assumption: our UK compliance content localises to the German regime with about 60% reuse — our CTO says it's more like 40%, and if he's right the engineering cost roughly doubles. Two existing customers (both UK banks with Frankfurt operations) have said they'd sponsor a pilot — I have the emails from May. Constraint: we cannot hire more than 8 people total next year, HR freeze from the board, and marketing spend is capped at £1.5m. There's a half-formed idea floating around that we partner with a local player like Regnology instead of going direct — nobody has scoped it, might be nothing. Also worth saying: our NRR is 112%, and if we just focused on expansion we might hit £16m without any new market — Priya's cohort model in the June board pack says £15.8m by FY28 on expansion alone. I honestly don't know whether the Germany window closes if we wait a year — two US competitors raised big rounds in Q2. The CFO wants to wait 12 months, the CRO wants to go now. So: Germany in 2027, or UK depth?

Need to decide how we take £4m out of opex by end of Q2 2027 — do we do it mainly through offshoring support, automation, or closing the Leeds office? Braindump before the exec offsite, apologies for the mess:

- context: 240 heads, £31m revenue, EBITDA minus £1.8m, board wants breakeven by Q3 2027, non-negotiable
- target: £4m annualised opex out, ideally £2.5m of it landed by end of Q2
- support org = 62 people, £2.9m/yr. Offshore quote from TaskUs: ~40% saving on 45 roles = ~£1.1m/yr, but CSAT risk is real
- when a competitor did this their Trustpilot dropped 4.1 to 3.3 in six months (I saw it in their public reviews, not exactly science)
- automation: the deflection pilot in April handled 34% of tickets end to end (our own dashboard, n=6 weeks). Jamie extrapolates that to £800k/yr saving but it assumes vendor pricing holds at renewal — the vendor contract renews in November and they know we're locked in
- Leeds office lease = £600k/yr, break clause March 2027. 70 people based there. Hybrid means maybe we don't need it at all? Nobody has modelled the attrition hit. My guess: we'd lose 10-15% of Leeds staff if we close — pure guess
- constraint: no more than one compulsory redundancy round in the next 12 months — we promised staff after the last one and the CEO is adamant
- constraint: engineering (58 heads) is ring-fenced, board agreed
- assumption: revenue flat at £31m. Sales says +8% but they said that last year and we did minus 2%
- half-formed: could we sell the Leeds sublease rights? or do a 3-day office share with WPP's local outfit? no idea if either is real
- Dana thinks we should just do a 10% across-the-board RIF and be done. I think that's how you kill morale twice — we disagree openly
- worry: doing all three at once = change saturation. The ops director says max two big changes in parallel, based on the 2024 migration mess
- unknown: what does offshoring do to our ISO 27001 posture? the renewal audit is January 2027

Trying to decide whether we bet the next two quarters on the AI copilot or finally do the platform rewrite. Or neither — I keep going back and forth, and I'm writing this partly to think. The goal I actually care about is 15% ARR growth next year without engineering attrition getting worse.

The copilot: the prototype demoed at SKO got the best reaction I've seen in years. Sales swears it would lift win rate from 22% to 30% — that number came from Marcus polling 15 AEs on Slack, so treat accordingly. Pricing thinks we could charge +£15/seat/month on our 40,000 seats, so up to £7.2m a year if attach were 100%, which it won't be — 25% attach feels honest, call it £1.8m. Build estimate is 4 engineers for 6 months. Actually, Elena's team said 6 engineers for 8 months once you include evals and the safety review — use hers, she's usually right. LLM serving cost is the thing nobody can pin down: finance modelled £3 per seat per month, could be half that or triple depending on caching. Assumption: our data-processing agreements let us send customer CRM text to a model provider — legal has NOT confirmed this, and if it's wrong the whole thing is dead in enterprise, which is 60% of revenue.

The rewrite: the platform is 9 years old, deploys take 45 minutes, and we lost two staff engineers to it last year — the exit interviews say so explicitly. Infra says the monolith adds roughly 30% drag to every feature — that's the number the CTO keeps quoting, source unclear, possibly the 2024 DX survey. Rewrite = 10 engineers, 12 months, and history says double whatever engineering estimates on this codebase. If we don't do it, copilot velocity sits on the same slow foundation — so maybe rewrite first, then copilot. But the window: three competitors shipped copilots in the last two quarters, PMM says we're 12 months behind already, and waiting a year might mean entering dead.

Budget: the board approved £2m for strategic initiatives. Realistically it's £1.2m after the security remediation eats its share, which it will. Deadline: the CEO said the copilot must demo at Camunda Days on 14 May 2027. Though honestly, if the rewrite is the right call the demo date shouldn't drive it — we could show smoke and mirrors. Second thought on revenue: I said 25% attach earlier, but enterprise procurement cycles mean year one is more like 10%, so £700k in year one — the £1.8m is a year-three number. The CPO wants the copilot, the CTO wants the rewrite, they've been at a standoff in every exec meeting since June, and I'm the tiebreak. Which way do we go?

We're a 40-person B2B SaaS company doing about £3.2m ARR, growing 15% a year, which is slower than we'd like. The board wants a plan by end of quarter. We're weighing three moves: expanding into the German market (probably £400k up front for localisation, sales hires and compliance — our CEO thinks it could add £800k ARR within 18 months but our head of sales thinks that's optimistic); doubling down on UK mid-market with a partner channel (cheaper, maybe £150k, but partners take a 25% cut and we've never run a channel before); or building the analytics add-on customers keep asking for (two quarters of engineering time, roughly £250k in payroll, might lift retention from 88% to 92% and support a 10% price rise). We can't fund more than one properly. Cash runway is about 14 months. The team is nervous about spreading ourselves thin, and honestly we disagree about how price-sensitive our customers actually are. What should we do?
Go ahead and draft the model.
Run analysis.

Our family-run logistics firm (120 drivers, £18m turnover, thin 4% margins) has to respond to the city's new clean-air zone within a year. We see three routes: replacing a third of the diesel fleet with electric vans now (about £2.1m capex, grants might cover 20%, but charging infrastructure at the depot is another £300k and our ops director doubts the range figures); paying the daily charges and passing costs to customers (roughly £190k a year, but two big contracts have clauses letting them exit if prices rise more than 5%); or subcontracting inner-city deliveries to a green courier (quotes suggest 12% of revenue on affected routes, we keep the trunk work, but we lose the customer relationship on the last mile). Diesel resale values are falling and nobody agrees how fast. The bank will lend but wants a plan. Which way should we jump?
The subcontractor cost should be 12% of revenue on the affected routes.
Set it to 0.12.
For the subcontracting option, set the effect value on Subcontractor cost as share of affected revenue to 0.12 — a share, no unit.

We need to decide whether to move our data platform off our current vendor. The options are staying put, moving to a cheaper competitor, or bringing it in-house. Migration risk worries the team, and the in-house route needs hiring we have not scoped. We have not put numbers on any of this yet. What is the smartest path?

We are a regional facilities-services firm, about 210 staff, mostly commercial cleaning and grounds maintenance across Yorkshire. Our biggest client, roughly a third of revenue, has told us they are putting the contract out to tender next spring. We are arguing about what to do: bid aggressively to keep it even if margins go to near zero; diversify fast by buying a small M&E maintenance firm we have been circling (the owner wants to retire, price not agreed, somewhere between £600k and £900k depending on who you ask); or invest in a sales push into the NHS estates market, which we have never sold into and whose procurement cycle scares us. Finance says cash is tight but will not put a number on it. The MD and the ops director disagree about whether we could even service NHS work with the current management layer. And nobody has agreed what success actually looks like — keeping revenue flat, protecting margin, or something else. We need a direction before the January board meeting.

I run product at a 60-person consumer fintech app, around 400k monthly actives, flat for six months. We can only staff one big bet properly this half and the exec team is split three ways. Growth wants to restart paid acquisition with a £300k budget — last time CAC blew out to £41 and we stopped, but they reckon with the new referral loop it lands nearer £25. The CEO wants to launch a paid premium tier at £7.99 a month; our own survey suggests maybe 4% of actives would convert in the first year, though nobody trusts the survey much. I want to rebuild onboarding instead: activation is 34% today, the redesign costs roughly £180k of engineering time over one quarter, and comparable fixes elsewhere lifted activation to around 45%. Retention is wobbling and the dashboards disagree about churn, which makes every argument circular. The board meets in six weeks and wants a single committed direction.
How do you decide which factors matter in the analysis?

We are a UK B2B SaaS company with 8 million pounds ARR selling compliance software to mid-market financial services firms. Growth has slowed from 40% to 18% year on year. We are deciding whether to move upmarket to enterprise banks, double down on mid-market with a lower-priced self-serve tier, or acquire a smaller competitor to buy market share. We have about 6 million pounds of cash and 18 months of runway. Which route should we take?
